channel.title: Mulder, It's Me
channel.description: Essays on The X-Files as film and television craft.

item.title: Series Order: What Hulu Actually Bought
item.description: Eight months after ordering a pilot, Hulu has picked up Ryan Coogler's X-Files to series. Sorting the confirmed from the reported from the rumored, and what the shape of the deal says about the show.

item.title: After the Basement: The Lesson Was the Failure
item.description: The X-Files is credited with the procedural-serial hybrid and a writers' room that produced half the showrunners of the 2000s. Its most powerful legacy was neither. It was the example of a great show that could not end, and the generation that built its own series to avoid becoming it.

item.title: The Case Against Mulder: I Want to Believe
item.description: The second X-Files film is remembered as the small one that opened behind The Dark Knight. Its real problem was braver than that. It is the only X-Files story that puts its hero's faith on trial and rules for the skeptic.

item.title: Two Solos: What the Leads Did With the Camera
item.description: Handed the director's chair, David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson each made the same decision. They removed the other one. What the four episodes say about a partnership seen from inside.

item.title: The Score Was the Monster
item.description: Mark Snow's music for The X-Files is remembered for a whistled theme. His real achievement was a weekly score that occupied the darkness the camera refused to show, which is why the two feature films, scored for orchestra, sound less like the show than any episode.

item.title: The Paranoid Style, Renewed Weekly
item.description: The X-Files took its parking garages and its shadows from the conspiracy thrillers of the 1970s, then quietly reversed what those films meant. Pakula's paranoia ended in defeat. Television needed paranoia that could come back next week.

item.title: Who Holds the Camera: The X-Files' Real Format Experiments
item.description: The show's famous rule-breaking episodes get lumped together as stunts. They are two different projects. One asserts the director's control of the image. The other, the more radical one, gives the camera away to someone who can't be trusted.

item.title: The Wrong Whale: Post-Modern Prometheus and the Bride
item.description: Chris Carter said his black-and-white fifth-season episode was an homage to the 1931 Frankenstein. Its framing device, its talking monster, its camp doctor and its rewritten ending all come from the sequel. Reading it against the right film explains why it works.

item.title: Triangle Is a Comedy, and the Long Take Is the Joke
item.description: Chris Carter sold his sixth-season stunt as Hitchcock. Watch where the unbroken camera actually comes alive and it looks like something else: a screwball farce, timed by a Steadicam instead of an editor.

item.title: Fight the Future Is Best When It Forgets It Is a Movie
item.description: The 1998 film spent its money on a spaceship under the ice and a helicopter over a cornfield. Its best scenes cost almost nothing, and they are the ones that still look like The X-Files.

item.title: Kim Manners Was Not a Horror Director
item.description: He directed more hours of The X-Files than anyone, and he is remembered for Home. But the thing the show kept asking him for was not fear. It was motion.

item.title: Los Angeles Made the Look a Choice
item.description: Fans remember the 1998 move from Vancouver as the moment The X-Files lost its atmosphere. The awards record and the episodes say the opposite: the show's photography only became a style once the weather stopped supplying it.

item.title: The Flashlight Is the Camera
item.description: The flashlight on The X-Files is usually described as a lighting style. It was something stranger: the show's only honest narrator, and the device that turned a network procedural into a first-person film.
